When you describe something as defunct, you mean it no longer exists, operates, or functions — and it never will again. It is completely finished. Whatever it once was or once did, it is no longer. The thing is gone for good.

That last part is important: defunct always implies permanence. Something defunct hasn't taken a break. It hasn't paused. It has permanently stopped being what it was.

Here's a subtle but crucial point that makes defunct special: the word quietly tells you that the thing used to exist or work. You would never call something defunct if it never functioned in the first place. So when you use this word, you are automatically saying two things at once — "this existed or worked once" and "it no longer does." That double meaning is baked into the word.
What Kinds of Things Can Be Defunct?

This word is flexible and can describe a wide range of things.

Organizations and institutions are the most common use. A company that has shut down and dissolved permanently is a defunct company. A school that has closed its doors forever is a defunct school. A political party that no longer exists is a defunct party.

Laws and systems can also be defunct. A law that has been formally abolished and is no longer in effect is a defunct law. A defunct system is one that has been dismantled or has simply stopped being used — and won't be revived.

Technologies and products can be defunct too. A software program that has been discontinued and is no longer supported or available is defunct. A product line that a company has permanently retired is defunct.

People, too, can technically be described as defunct, meaning deceased — but this usage is uncommon and sounds quite formal or even literary. In everyday speech, you would almost never call a person defunct; you'd simply say they passed away or died.

Defunct has a slightly formal and neutral tone. It doesn't carry deep emotion the way words like "destroyed" or "dead" might. It is matter-of-fact. When you say something is defunct, you are simply stating a cold reality: whatever it was, it is over. Because of this tone, you'll often see it used in journalism, business writing, legal contexts, and formal discussions.
How Defunct Differs From Similar Words

Several words are close to defunct in meaning, but they are not the same.

Inactive means something is not currently doing anything, but it could start again. A defunct thing cannot. This is the most important distinction. Something inactive is sleeping; something defunct is gone.

Obsolete means something has become outdated and replaced by something better or newer, but it may technically still exist. A defunct thing doesn't just exist somewhere gathering dust — it has completely ceased to be. For example, fax machines are arguably obsolete, but they aren't defunct because they still exist and are still used in some places. Meanwhile, a fax company that shut down years ago is defunct.

Closed is a simpler, more everyday word that often describes temporary or permanent shutdowns of businesses or places. Defunct specifically implies permanence and often a complete dissolution — not just the doors being locked, but the organization itself ceasing to exist entirely.

Dissolved is close, but it is a verb and typically applies only to organizations. Defunct is broader and works as a describing word across many types of things.

"The passengers were stranded because the airline they had booked with was now defunct."
Here, the airline has permanently ceased to exist — not just suspended flights.

"He worked for a defunct tech startup that ran out of funding and shut down."
The startup no longer exists at all.

"Many defunct laws from the 19th century were never officially removed from the books."
These laws are no longer in effect — they have no power or use.

"She collected merchandise from defunct fast-food chains that no one remembered anymore."
The chains had permanently gone out of business.
If you want to remember this word in its simplest form: defunct describes something that once existed or worked, but has now permanently stopped doing so — it is finished, gone, and not coming back.
